items.title: Google ships Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API — load tool schemas on demand instead of stuffing them all into every prompt
items.summary: Add a tool_search tool and set defer_loading:true on your other tools; the model still sees the name and description of every deferred tool, but the full parameter schema only loads when the model asks for that tool by name, inside the same request. interaction.steps shows exactly which tool got searched and loaded, and deferred schemas stay out of the cached prompt prefix so prefix caching still works turn to turn.
items.why: If your agent juggles dozens of tools, this is a direct fix for the token bloat and tool-misselection problem that comes from cramming every schema into context on every call.
items.action: Add tool_search + defer_loading:true to your long-tail, rarely-used tools in the Interactions API and keep your most-used ones undeferred, then check interaction.steps to see what actually got searched.

eval.reason: Genuine new API capability (tool_search/defer_loading) solving a real agent-scaling problem, not pricing/benchmark/partnership. Confirmed not a duplicate via grep across all available prior briefs.

items.title: swyx flags an OpenRouter routing leak — some providers were quietly forwarding requests to MiniMax without saying so
items.summary: A researcher's canary links sent through OpenRouter resurfaced via MiniMax 40 to 130 hours later, meaning AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake were silently routing requests to MiniMax even when a different provider was selected — and someone opened those links, meaning outputs were accessible to whoever did.
items.why: Picking a specific provider on a multi-provider gateway doesn't guarantee that provider is actually who sees your prompts and outputs — this is a real instance of that assumption breaking.
items.action: If you route through OpenRouter or any multi-provider gateway, check your provider-pinning/allow-list settings rather than trusting the provider label shown in the UI.

items.title: Harrison Chase: how LangChain builds a “knowledge factory” to make its own internal agents actually useful
items.summary: Breaks the knowledge an agent needs into three buckets — skills (how to do things your way), domain knowledge (how the business works), and data-access guidance (where to look) — and describes how LangChain's own LangSmith Engine and internal GTM/content agents run on exactly this pattern in production.
items.why: His core point is blunt and useful: more context doesn't fix a dumb agent, better-curated reusable knowledge does — and he's describing what that looks like at his own company, not a hypothetical.
items.action: Map your own coding agent's recent failures against those three buckets; most “the agent didn't know X” bugs turn out to be a missing skill doc or domain-knowledge gap, not a model limitation.
